answer:
**The CPU can enqueue GPU work before that work has finished.** This asynchronous execution allows launch and preparation to overlap device computation. Requesting a Python number with `.item()` requires the device result to be available on the host, so the CPU may have to wait. [1](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/index.html)

Imagine each step queues kernels and immediately reads its loss scalar. That read creates a repeated synchronization point, reducing the opportunity to overlap work across the pipeline. Printing actual device values can create a similar need to retrieve them.

**The effect depends on frequency and workload.** One occasional scalar read does not universally destroy throughput. A repeated read in a tight small-kernel loop may be much more costly. Accumulate metrics on-device and transfer summaries at planned intervals when appropriate.

Use CUDA events or properly synchronized timing for benchmarks. Measuring only the time to enqueue an operation can make GPU work look falsely cheap, while a later `.item()` appears to bear the cost of all preceding work. A timeline helps attribute the delay to the real computation and synchronization boundary.

**Technical details and references.**

CUDA operations are usually asynchronous relative to the CPU. Reading a device scalar with `.item()` or formatting device tensor values for printing requires the value on the host, introducing synchronization and breaking useful overlap. [1](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/index.html)

The cost depends on context; one occasional scalar read does not universally “destroy” throughput, but doing it every step can create repeated stalls. Accumulate metrics on-device, log less frequently, and transfer batches of summaries at planned boundaries. Use proper CUDA events or synchronized timing for benchmarks; otherwise asynchronous execution can make a slow operation appear deceptively cheap.
